sentences.text: Xenacanthus is an extinct genus of xenacanthid shark named after its distinctive spine.
This animal possessed a thin, elongated body with a dorsal fin extending from the head to the tip of its triangular tail.
A spine ran along the entire body of Xenacanthus, stretching from the skull to the tip of the tail.
It featured a ribbonlike dorsal fin that ran the entire length of its back and joined the anal fin at the tail.
The spine-like structures of Xenacanthus allowed its fossils to be preserved in better condition than those of other sharks because bone preserves better than cartilage.
Researchers speculate that the distinctive spine of Xenacanthus may have been venomous, similar to a sting ray.
The genus Xenacanthus was first described by Beyrich in 1848.
Xenacanthus likely swam in a manner similar to modern conger eels due to its fin arrangement.
Isotopic measurements indicate Xenacanthus was a euryoecious genus inhabiting rivers, oligotrophic lakes, and eutrophic lakes.
Xenacanthus decheni grew to about 1 meter, while X. meisenheimensis reached up to 1.2 meters.
Xenacanthus parallelus was one of the smallest species, with fully grown males reaching 20 cm and females 34 cm.
Xenacanthus belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, subclass Elasmobranchii, order Xenacanthiformes, and family Xenacanthidae.
Pleuracanthus is a synonym for the genus Xenacanthus.
Xenacanthus lived from the Pennsylvanian to the Permian, until about 280 million years ago.
The time range for Xenacanthus is from the Moscovian to the Norian, between 312.8 and 205.7 million years ago.
Xenacanthus fossils are known from the Carboniferous-Permian periods in North America, Europe, and South America.
Xenacanthus lived in New Mexico, United States.
